claims.text: HEAs naturally exhibit local lattice distortions because of their compositional complexity.
The dynamic strength–ductility balance of HEAs is governed by crystallographic orientation-dependent dislocation nucleation and cross-slip.
Intrinsic local lattice distortions mediate the orientation dependence of dislocation nucleation and cross-slip.
Local lattice distortions lower dislocation-activity energy barriers along favorable slip directions.
Lower dislocation-activity barriers enable more uniformly distributed plastic deformation.
Local lattice distortions promote cross-slip events.
Under uniaxial loading, local lattice distortions preferentially lower dislocation-nucleation barriers for certain crystallographic orientations.
Orientation-dependent barrier lowering enhances dislocation mobility and cross-slip.
Enhanced dislocation mobility and cross-slip produce more distributed plastic deformation.
Distributed plastic deformation is a mechanism for balancing high strength and ductility.
Relative to the proposed baseline, loading an HEA along a favorable orientation should modestly increase yield strength.
Relative to the proposed baseline, loading an HEA along a favorable orientation should markedly increase strain-to-failure.
The predicted effects should occur from room temperature to approximately 500 K at strain rates of about 10^7 to 10^9 s^-1.
The hypothesis applies to HEAs with enough compositional randomness to generate significant local lattice distortions.
The hypothesis may not apply to alloys with insufficient compositional complexity or outside the specified temperature and high-strain-rate regime.
MD timescale and system-size limitations make the quantitative strength and ductility differences uncertain.
The results may vary with alloy chemistry and simulation parameters.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says favorable orientations lower dislocation-nucleation barriers, while the predicted outcome says those orientations modestly increase yield strength. No additional strengthening mechanism is supplied to reconcile easier nucleation with higher yield strength.
